You answer an analyst's questions about SITIME Corp using only the numbered sources below: passages from the company's annual report (Form 10-K) and transcripts of its earnings calls.

Rules:
- Use only what the sources state. No outside knowledge, no guessing, and no numbers the sources don't give (don't compute growth rates or totals yourself).
- Every sentence of your answer needs support: one or more quotes, each copied exactly, character for character, from one source, with that source's label. Quote the clause that states the fact, at most about 40 words. Don't fix typos or join text from different places.
- If the sources don't answer the question, set answerable to false and return no sentences. Don't answer a different question than the one asked, and don't accept a premise of the question that the sources don't support.
- Lead with the direct answer. Use one to four sentences. Write in the third person (name the company, or "it"), not in the filing's "we" and "our".
- Say who said it when the source is a call ("Michele Buck said..."). Call transcripts are machine transcriptions and may contain errors; quote them as written.

Sources:

To answer your second question first, we do need a new mask set, but sometimes those are very similar. they're not the the the design of the resonator is not very different for example between a 24 megahertz and a 26 megahertz it's not going to be very different however between a 24 megahertz and uh 76.8 megahertz i think it could be different uh but uh generally the good news is that the resonator industry has worked around the quartz limitations in the past, and there are basically a handful, maybe two handfuls, so call it a dozen, quote-unquote, popular frequencies that exist. And so I think that makes our task easier as we go from one frequency to the other. And you're absolutely right. The requirement for frequencies beyond, say, 75 megahertz increases.

[S2] 10-K: Item 1. Business
Key Building Blocks of Timing Solutions

Timing solutions comprise three key building blocks: resonators, oscillators, and clock ICs. While simpler systems generally require only an external resonator coupled with a basic embedded oscillator circuit, more complex systems require advanced timing solutions that may integrate a variety of resonators, oscillators, and clock ICs in a single chip package. The complexity of these timing solutions increases significantly when the performance requirements of the systems that use them increase, such as electronic systems required to support the 5G communication network infrastructure.

The key building blocks of SiTime’s timing solutions are:

• Resonators – mechanical silicon structures that vibrate at a precise frequency and provide the core accuracy and stability in oscillator systems;

• Oscillators – active systems that combine resonators with analog mixed-signal ICs that cause the resonators to vibrate, generating accurate and stable clock signals; and

• Clock ICs – integrated analog mixed-signal circuits that use phase-locked loops (“PLLs”), clock dividers, and drivers, and have multiple clock signals on the output of the system. Clock ICs require resonators and oscillators for timing references and may integrate these components into complex systems.

These three building blocks may be used individually or in combination, depending on the end product’s performance, price, and size requirements.

Given our broad knowledge of timing market solutions across all three categories, we believe our system-level timing solutions save customer design time, increase their end products' performance and reliability, while also reducing their overall board footprint, creating value. Moving to 5G. In 5G, the opportunities available to SITAM continue to drive the company's expansion into the communications market. Our products continue to see solid design traction in 5G applications at Tier 1 manufacturers of telecommunications equipment. In addition, we had previously mentioned ORAN, which is Open Radio Access Networks, and we continue to see significant interest in ORAN hardware solutions that are being developed for greenfield operators as well as the traditional carriers. ORAN is getting traction because it gives operators best-in-class equipment and performance while driving better deployment economics. And the need for successful interoperability of equipment from different suppliers is a driving factor for side-time success. We're getting significant traction with O-RAN customers worldwide across the entire radio networks, including RRUs, small cells, and distributed units. In the area of 5G optical transport, where we are engaged with 100 to 800G optical and SOC suppliers with our SIT 9501 products, we find that we are able to offer unique value with high performance in the smallest form factor. In conclusion, SciTime is uniquely positioned to disrupt the market as the first company that continues to provide system-level timing solution.

Rajesh Vashist: Yeah, our SAM is still around a billion to a billion point two. It might be a little bit higher depending on when we introduce products and so on, but it's certainly less than two billion. It's also mostly concentrated right now in oscillators. So while we do have resonators that have been introduced, While we do have analog clocking solutions that have been introduced, our ramp into that from a revenue point of view, we have already set expectations, will be relatively slow. I think our entry into these markets is significant for customers in the following way, in the way that they can then come and have conversations with us on all of these products. And not every customer wants to talk to us about every one of them. Sometimes they want to talk to us only about resonators or oscillators or clocking, and then that becomes an entry point to talking about other products. So from a TAM point of view, we're still pretty tiny, you know, $1.5 billion in TAM out of an $8 billion total market. SAM at $1.5 billion, SAM out of an $8 billion total TAM. And, of course, CyTimes revenue is still pretty small in comparison at around $100 million. So we still, even if we maintained and did not grow our SAM very much, we would still probably have a long way to go before we fill out those boots.
